3 Reasons CRM is Risky and 1 Stock to Buy Instead

Over the past six months, Salesforce has been a great trade, beating the S&P 500 by 19.8%. Its stock price has climbed to $239.80, representing a healthy 28.7% increase. This was partly due to its solid quarterly results, and the run-up might have investors contemplating their next move.

Is there a buying opportunity in Salesforce, or does it present a risk to your portfolio? Get the full breakdown from our expert analysts, it's free.

Why Is Salesforce Not Exciting?

We're happy investors have made money, but we don't have much confidence in Salesforce. Here are three reasons you should be careful with CRM, plus one stock we'd rather own.

1. Weak Billings Point to Soft Demand

Billings is a non-GAAP metric that is often called "cash revenue" because it shows how much money the company has collected from customers in a certain period. This is different from revenue, which must be recognized in pieces over the length of a contract.

Salesforce's billings came in at $9.77 billion in Q2, and over the last four quarters, its year-on-year growth averaged 11.2%. This performance was underwhelming and suggests that increasing competition is causing challenges in acquiring/retaining customers.

Salesforce Billings
2. Projected Revenue Growth Is Slim

Forecasted revenues by Wall Street analysts signal a company's potential. Predictions may not always be accurate, but accelerating growth typically boosts valuation multiples and stock prices while slowing growth does the opposite.

Over the next 12 months, sell-side analysts expect Salesforce's revenue to rise by 10.4%, close to its 13.3% annualized growth for the past five years. This projection doesn't excite us and suggests its newer products and services will not accelerate its top-line performance yet.

3. Operating Margin in Limbo

While many software businesses point investors to their adjusted profits, which exclude stock-based compensation (SBC), we prefer GAAP operating margin because SBC is a legitimate expense used to attract and retain talent. This is one of the best measures of profitability because it shows how much money a company takes home after developing, marketing, and selling its products.

Looking at the trend in its profitability, Salesforce's operating margin might have fluctuated slightly but has generally stayed the same over the last two years. This raises questions about the company's expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability. Its operating margin for the trailing 12 months was 19.9%.

Salesforce (CRM) Is ‘Sticky’ In The AI Era, Jim Cramer Said & Remarked That Amateurs Can Beat Adobe
Ramish Cheema

CRM

Trading disclosure

Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) and Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) are two stocks that Jim Cramer frequently discusses. For both, most of his remarks are about AI and the role that the firms are playing in the sector. The CNBC TV host has frequently defended Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and his artificial intelligence initiatives and discussed the impact of AI on Adobe. In his morning appearance on the 12th, Cramer continued to comment on Adobe's business model and whether it could withstand the competitive pressures in the age of easy software development fueled by artificial intelligence:

"Now also. We also have a double downgrade of Adobe. That's Wells Fargo, Salesforce was Bank of America. What I think what's most interesting, Adobe is easier to copy and I think people have been doing it. You and I discussed that in the break. Adobe's very expensive. People feel that perhaps it is no longer worth this much. Because of Claude. Because of ChatGPT. . .the 660 dollar. Now this is very interesting David. Salesforce had a fantastic Dreamforce and a great quarter. And people are kind of coming around to think that maybe there's no disintermediation, that it's really Monday.com, smaller outfits, Hubspot. What's interesting is that the guy did wait, the analyst did wait till it came back. So it wasn't like a, well I bought it at the top situation. A lot of it has to do with what's sticky. And what's not. And Salesforce is regarded as very sticky, it gets in the organization, people like it when they use it. And Adobe is regarded as being easy to disrupt, whether it be from Canva, whether it be from Figma, whether it be from, the, I don't know, I subscribe to Adobe and I just find that, you can kind of fool around with it on an amateur basis and beat it."

Cramer's faith in Salesforce has been rewarding. The shares are up by 20% since late August after closing 22% higher on August 27th. Ahead of the gain, the CNBC TV host discussed Salesforce in detail, which we covered as part of Jim Cramer Discussed These 22 Stocks Including A Hidden Oil & Energy Play.

Jim Cramer Sees a Telling Change in Broadcom’s (AVGO) Stock

For Salesforce, Cramer built on the earlier comments we've linked above. He extended his take to outline that Salesforce was sticky with businesses and was making durable inroads into businesses. The remarks are central to the firm's hypothesis as for Salesforce, the debate has centered around the durability and popularity of its AI initiatives.

On this front, the firm's second quarter earnings saw its Agentforce platform's annual recurring revenue grow by a massive 240% annually to touch $1.5 billion. The Agentforce growth validates what Cramer's been 'hearing' as it indicates that the AI platform is making inroads into the business world. As for the 'stickiness', current remaining performance obligations (cRPO), which measures revenue from signed and contracted customer agreements for the next 12 months, grew by 14% annually to touch $33.5 billion. Zooming specifically on AI, during the earnings call, chief revenue officer Miguel Milano outlined that "Customers that start the agentic journey with Salesforce, on average, they are already at double the AOV with a perspective of nearly quadrupling, 3x-4x the AOV." AOV is annual order value and Milano's comments indicate that AI is making a real impact on the income statement.

Key Stats for Salesforce Stock

Street Target: ~$286

Potential Total Return: ~81%

Annualized IRR: ~15% / year

What Happened?

Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) closed at $246.74 on October 15, 2026, up 4.57% on the day and 34.08% above its July 31 close of $184.02. Most of that run came on August 27, when shares jumped 22.58% after second-quarter results. The October 15 close sits 2.11% below that day's $252.05.

No Salesforce-specific catalyst was confirmed for October 15. The gain came with the sector: ServiceNow (NOW) closed up 6.14% as investors rotated into enterprise software amid a sell-off in semiconductor shares.

Evidence from Salesforce's September investor session, available through its investor relations materials, suggests AI usage is running ahead of what Salesforce bills for it.

Salesforce Drawdowns (TIKR)
Salesforce's Top AI Customers Roughly Doubled Their ARR, but Billing Trails Usage

Robin Washington, President and Chief Operating and Financial Officer, spoke about the top 100 customers by Agentic Work Units, Salesforce's measure of the work its agents complete. Among them, she said, "within 18 months of Agentforce's launch, we're seeing ARR uplift about 2x as to what it was." As customers become agentic enterprises, she sees "a 3x to 4x opportunity for that ARR uplift" over several years.

The cohort is selected by usage, and Washington did not limit the annual recurring revenue figure to AI products. It shows what is possible, not what the average customer pays.

The lag comes from contract design. President and Chief Revenue Officer Alexa Vignone said that in Q2, "7 of our 10 largest deals were AELAs." AELAs are flat, seat-based agentic enterprise license agreements. President and Chief Operating Officer Miguel Milano added that "Contract lengths are increasing." In January, a Gartner analyst said she expects these capped deals to convert into defined-quantity contracts at renewal. Salesforce responded that its consumption-based AI pricing is tied to business outcomes.

Adecco and Siemens Show Where Repricing Comes From

Adecco Group (ADEN) runs 7 agents in 12 countries. Pierre Matuchet, its Senior Vice President of IT, said those agents cut the time to present candidates by 40% and lifted its fill rate by 10%. Adecco has decided to roll out Coworker to 27,000 users, which Milano said it could switch on under an edition it already owned.

Separately, Adecco's two-year AELA, signed seven months before the session, carries "unlimited credit for all these use cases." Milano's renewal pitch: "What if we agree on a couple of metrics and then we share in your success?" That is a proposal, not a signed contract.

Recent moves in Salesforce's share price tell a mixed story. Most Popular Narrative: 4% Undervalued

Against a last close of $246.74, the most followed fair value on Salesforce sits near $255.90. According to michaelyang, this leaves a small discount that hinges less on aggressive forecasts and more on simple survival.

The per-seat licence was only ever the toll booth. The asset is the governed system of record: every customer, every deal, every entitlement, for about 80% of the Fortune 500. And the one thing an autonomous AI agent cannot do is act on a customer without getting into that record first. An agent with no permissions, no governance and no audit trail is not an asset, it is a liability waiting to happen. So the same automation wave that threatens the seat count is exactly what drives every serious enterprise deeper into the data layer Salesforce owns. The meter changes from per-person to per-action. It does not disappear.
